title: KV cache reference-count leak: root cause analysis and mitigation plan
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Summary: During a traffic spike on 2026-02-26 we observed sustained memory growth on several serving hosts leading to OOM restarts and degraded throughput. Root cause: a reference-counting bug in the KV/prefix cache that allowed stale cache nodes to retain references after eviction paths failed when concurrent iterator invalidation occurred. This manifested as leaked entries which kept bulky KV caches pinned in memory and prevented expected reclamation by the eviction worker. The leak was not triggered by normal traffic patterns and required a particular interleaving of batch reads, background flushes, and eviction scanning under high concurrency. Impact: 12 hosts restarted over 3 hours, several customer requests experienced increased latency and a handful of internal canaries tripped. Incident detection and mitigation steps: on-call added temporary memory-based circuit breaker, reduced per-host cache size limit, and rolled a hotfix that made the eviction worker synchronous for a single shard to avoid iterator races.

root_cause: Reference-counting invariants were violated when the eviction iterator concurrently removed nodes while a batch read path temporarily re-established references. The iterator's expected lifecycle assumed single-writer semantics; under heavy concurrency the code path skipped decrementing a node's refcount, leaving it permanently pinned. This was exacerbated by missing unit tests for concurrent eviction/lookup interleavings and weak instrumentation around refcount metrics.
decision_log: Short-term: implement memory-based circuit breaker and lower cache soft limits to stop OOMs (approved by SRE)
Medium-term: change eviction worker to use a safe ticketing mechanism that prevents iterator invalidation races; serialized per-shard eviction as interim fix
Long-term: add per-key generation tags, switch to epoch-based reclamation to remove dependence on fine-grained refcounts, and harden tests with deterministic concurrency fuzz harnesses

notes: Mitigation prioritized minimizing user impact while we developed a correctness-first fix
We chose serialized eviction as an interim fix because it minimized code churn and had a fast rollback path
Longer-term epoch reclamation is preferred for scalability and will be benchmarked in a separate spike
